11910: Parched means extremely dry — so dry that it desperately needs water or moisture. The key word here is extremely. "Parched" is never used for something that is just slightly dry. It describes a serious, intense, almost painful lack of moisture. Think of the driest thing you can imagine — cracked desert ground under a blazing sun — and you're thinking of something parched.
The Two Main Ways "Parched" Is Used

1. To Describe Things and Places

When used for objects, land, or the environment, "parched" describes something that has lost almost all its moisture, usually because of intense heat or a long period without rain.

  • The parched earth cracked open under the summer heat.
  • The farmer looked sadly at the parched fields — not a drop of rain had fallen in weeks.
  • He ran his tongue over his parched lips, but there was no moisture left.
  • The hikers crossed a parched, dusty valley with no sign of water anywhere.

In these cases, you can almost see and feel the dryness. Parched land is not just a little dry — it is baked, cracked, and lifeless, starving for water. Parched lips are not just chapped — they are extremely dry and uncomfortable.

2. To Describe a Person (Extremely Thirsty)

When used for a person, "parched" means desperately thirsty — so thirsty that you feel an urgent need for water right now. This comes from the same idea: just as land becomes parched from lack of water, a person becomes parched when their body is starving for water.

  • After running for an hour in the heat, I was absolutely parched.
  • "Could I have a glass of water, please? I'm parched!" she said.
  • The soldiers marched through the desert, parched and exhausted.

This usage is very common in everyday conversation. When someone says "I'm parched," it simply means "I am very, very thirsty."

This is the most important thing to understand about "parched": it is always an extreme state. It is not a mild or moderate dryness. Compare:

  • Dry → some moisture is missing.
  • Very dry → noticeably lacking in moisture.
  • Parched → so severely dry that water is desperately needed, almost like a cry for relief.

If you say the grass is dry, it might just need watering. If you say the grass is parched, you picture it brown, brittle, and dying.
What Causes Something to Be Parched?

The most common cause is heat — especially prolonged, intense heat like a drought, a desert, or a blazing summer. However, a lack of rain alone (even without heat) can parch the land over time. For a person, physical exertion, hot weather, illness, or simply not drinking enough water can leave them parched. Occasionally, non-heat causes apply too — a person might have a parched throat after talking for hours or after a fever.
What Does "Parched" Look and Feel Like?

This is a word loaded with sensory detail. It paints a vivid picture:

  • Visually: cracked ground, brown and withered plants, dusty landscapes, dry and flaky skin or lips.
  • To the touch: rough, brittle, crumbly — like something that would fall apart if it got any drier.
  • As a feeling: an urgent, uncomfortable, almost desperate thirst — a scratchy, dry sensation in the throat.

When writers use "parched," they are trying to make you feel that dryness, not just understand it intellectually.

You will very often see "parched" used alongside these words, which helps you recognize it in context:

  • Parched earth / land / soil / ground — extremely dry terrain.
  • Parched lips / throat — extremely dry body parts craving moisture.
  • Parched landscape / desert / fields — a dry, desolate environment.
  • Absolutely / completely parched — intensifiers used when describing a very thirsty person.

• Dry is neutral and general. Parched is extreme and urgent. Your hair can be "dry." A dying desert is "parched."
  • Thirsty (for people) is mild. Parched is intense. You might feel "thirsty" before lunch. After a long run in the heat with no water, you feel "parched."
  • Arid is a more technical or geographical word used mainly for climates and regions (an arid climate). "Parched" is more vivid and emotional, and can apply to small things like lips or a throat, not just whole regions.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Parched" is slightly literary and expressive. It is perfectly natural in everyday conversation ("I'm parched — let's grab a drink!"), but it also appears frequently in books, poetry, and descriptive writing because it paints such a powerful picture. When you use "parched," you are not just stating a fact — you are conveying urgency, discomfort, and a deep need for water. It has an almost emotional weight to it.

Parched = extremely dry (for things/places) OR extremely thirsty (for people). It always signals an intense, severe lack of moisture — never a mild one. It often involves heat as the cause and carries a sense of desperate need for water.
11911: Parchment is a thin, flat sheet made from the treated skin of an animal — most commonly a sheep, goat, or calf — that people historically used as a surface for writing. Think of it as nature's version of paper, invented long before paper existed.
What It Is and How It's Made

To make parchment, the animal's skin is first soaked in water to soften it. Then it is stretched tightly across a wooden frame, scraped smooth with a special blade to remove hair, fat, and uneven patches, and left to dry under tension. As it dries while being held tight, it becomes thin, flat, pale, and firm — a surface clean and smooth enough to write on with ink.

The result is not leather (leather is tanned, meaning chemically preserved; parchment is simply cleaned, stretched, and dried). Parchment has its own distinct character: it is stiffer and lighter in color than leather, with a somewhat stiff, papery, and slightly waxy feel.

Parchment is typically cream-colored, off-white, or yellowish — never bright white. It has an old, warm, slightly aged look even when new. In bright light, you can sometimes see faint shadows where veins ran through the animal's skin. This is completely natural and is actually a sign of genuine, high-quality parchment.

For well over a thousand years — from roughly ancient times through the Middle Ages — parchment was the writing material of choice across much of the world, especially in Europe and the Middle East. Paper as we know it hadn't reached those regions yet, and earlier materials like clay tablets or papyrus (made from a plant) had significant limitations. Parchment was superior in many ways:

  • It was durable. Real parchment can survive for centuries — even millennia — under the right conditions. This is why we still have ancient religious manuscripts, legal charters, and hand-copied books from over a thousand years ago.
  • It could be scraped clean and reused if needed. A surface that was erased and rewritten on is called a palimpsest — a fascinating quirk of parchment's nature.
  • It was flexible enough to fold and bind into books, making it ideal for the early codex (the book format we still use today).

Kings, governments, churches, and scholars used parchment for their most important documents — royal decrees, religious scriptures, land deeds, laws, and sacred texts. The Magna Carta, for example, was written on parchment.
The Three Main Senses of the Word

The word "parchment" is used in three overlapping senses today:

1. The raw writing material itself
This is the original meaning — the actual sheet of animal skin, as described above. You might encounter this sense in historical or literary contexts: "The monk carefully unrolled the parchment and began to read."

2. An important document or certificate
Because parchment was historically the material used for official, formal, and permanent documents, the word "parchment" eventually came to mean any such important document — even if it isn't written on animal skin at all. Diplomas, royal charters, deeds, and legal documents are all called "parchments" in this sense. This is a figurative or extended use of the word, but it is entirely standard.

For example: "He received his parchment after four years of study" simply means he received his diploma or degree certificate.

3. Paper made to look and feel like parchment
Today, a thick, slightly cream-colored, stiff paper that resembles traditional animal-skin parchment is also called parchment (or parchment paper). It is used for printing certificates, formal letters, wedding invitations, and legal documents — because the appearance gives a feeling of formality, tradition, and prestige, even though it is ordinary paper.

There is also a separate product known as parchment paper in cooking — a heat-resistant, non-stick paper used in baking to line trays and prevent food from sticking. This gets its name from a slight visual resemblance to traditional parchment, but it is chemically treated paper and has nothing to do with animal skin. This usage is worth knowing simply to avoid confusion when you encounter the term in a kitchen or recipe context.

You will often see the word vellum used alongside "parchment." Vellum is essentially a finer, higher-quality form of parchment made specifically from the skins of very young animals — newborn calves, lambs, or kids (baby goats). Because the skin of young animals is thinner, smoother, and finer in texture, vellum produces an even more delicate and beautiful writing surface. Historically, the most precious manuscripts and the most important royal documents were written on vellum, not ordinary parchment.

In casual modern usage, the two words are often used interchangeably. But technically, all vellum is parchment, while not all parchment is vellum.

SenseWhat It Means

To put it plainly:

  • Parchment is writing material made from animal skin, stretched and dried until smooth and thin.
  • By extension, it can mean any important formal document, regardless of what it's actually made of.
  • It can also refer to paper that looks like the original material — used for certificates and formal printing.
  • In kitchens, parchment paper is a heat-resistant baking liner, a very different product sharing only the name.

The unifying idea across all these senses is the same: something that carries the feel — literally or figuratively — of importance, permanence, and formality. That is what parchment has always represented.
11912:
A pardon is an act of official forgiveness — specifically, forgiveness that removes or cancels a punishment. It is not just any forgiveness between people; it is always granted by someone in a position of authority, and it has real, formal consequences.

Think of it this way: if someone in power says, "This person was found guilty of a crime, but I am choosing to forgive them and free them from the consequences of that crime" — that act, and the document or decision behind it, is called a pardon.
The Primary Meaning: A Legal/Official Pardon

This is the most important and most commonly used meaning of the word "pardon" as a noun.

A pardon is an official decision made by a high authority — such as a President, a Governor, a King, or a Queen — to forgive a person for a crime and release them from all or part of the punishment they were sentenced to face.

Example: The president granted a pardon to the prisoner who had spent ten years in jail.

Here, "pardon" refers to the official act of forgiveness itself.

What does a pardon actually do?

A pardon can do several things, depending on how it is issued:

  • It can free a person from prison, even before their sentence is complete.
  • It can remove fines or other penalties the person was ordered to pay or face.
  • It can restore rights that a person lost because of their conviction — for example, in many countries, criminals lose the right to vote or hold public office. A pardon can give those rights back.
  • It can clear a person's name — especially useful in cases where someone was wrongly convicted, or where the law under which they were convicted is later seen as unjust.

Who can grant a pardon?

A pardon must come from someone with the recognized authority to grant one. It cannot come from just anyone. Common examples:

  • In India, the President has the power to grant pardons for offenses against central (union) law, including those punishable by death. Governors of states can pardon offenses against state law.
  • In the United States, the President can pardon any federal crime. State governors can pardon state crimes.
  • In the United Kingdom, the King or Queen grants pardons, acting on the advice of ministers.

This authority is usually written into a country's constitution or laws.
A Crucial Distinction: What a Pardon Is NOT

This is very important for understanding the word precisely. A pardon is often confused with other legal concepts. Here is how it is different:

Pardon vs. Acquittal

An acquittal means the court found the person not guilty — in other words, "you did not commit the crime."

A pardon means "you committed the crime (or were convicted of it), but the punishment is forgiven."

So an acquittal says the person is innocent. A pardon says the person was found guilty, but they are forgiven. These are very different. A pardon does not say the person is innocent.

Pardon vs. Commutation

A commutation reduces a punishment but does not forgive the crime. For example, a death sentence might be commuted to life imprisonment — the punishment is reduced, but the person is still convicted and still being punished.

A pardon goes further: it forgives the crime entirely and removes the punishment altogether (or most of it).

Pardon vs. Amnesty

Amnesty is similar to a pardon, but it is usually granted to a large group of people at once — often for political crimes or in the context of war.

A pardon is typically granted to a specific individual.

1. Full Pardon

A full pardon completely forgives the crime and its consequences. It restores the person's civil rights and releases them from all penalties. This is the most complete form.

2. Conditional Pardon

A conditional pardon is granted only if the person meets certain conditions. For example, a person might receive a pardon on the condition that they leave the country, stay out of trouble, or complete community service. If they break the conditions, the pardon can be withdrawn.

3. Posthumous Pardon

A posthumous pardon is granted to someone who has already died. This is typically done to restore the reputation of a person who was wrongly convicted or treated unjustly during their lifetime.

Example: Alan Turing, the British mathematician and war hero who was chemically castrated for being gay — which was a crime at the time — received a posthumous pardon decades after his death, when the law was recognized as deeply unjust.

4. Preemptive (or Prospective) Pardon

Some authorities have the power to grant a pardon before a person has even been tried or convicted. This is called a preemptive or prospective pardon. It is controversial, but it has happened.

Example: In 1974, US President Gerald Ford granted a preemptive pardon to former President Richard Nixon for any crimes Nixon may have committed during the Watergate scandal — before Nixon was ever charged or tried.
An Important Nuance: Does a Pardon Mean Innocence?

No, it does not.

A pardon forgives punishment. It does not declare innocence. The conviction, in many cases, still remains on the record. The legal and historical record still says the person was found guilty — the pardon simply says that the punishment has been removed.

However, in some legal systems, a full pardon can come with the clearing of one's criminal record (sometimes called expungement), meaning the conviction is also wiped from official records. But this depends on the country and the specific terms of the pardon.

In less formal, everyday contexts, the word pardon as a noun can also mean a simple act of excusing someone for a minor offense or mistake — essentially, forgiveness at the personal level.

Example: "He bowed his head and asked for her pardon after accidentally bumping into her."

Here, "pardon" means the forgiveness he was requesting. However, this usage is less common today in everyday speech (we are more likely to say "forgiveness" or "apology" in casual conversation). You will mostly encounter this sense in older or more formal writing.

To bring it all together:

A pardon (noun) is an official act of forgiveness granted by a person in authority that forgives a crime and removes punishment. It does not say the person is innocent — it says the punishment is cancelled. It can be full or conditional, given to an individual while alive or posthumously, and sometimes even granted before a conviction. It is different from an acquittal (which means "not guilty"), a commutation (which only reduces punishment), and an amnesty (which is for groups, not individuals). In rare, more formal or literary usage, it can also mean personal forgiveness for a minor social offense.
11913:
To pardon someone means to choose not to hold something against them — to release them from blame, punishment, or resentment, even when a wrong has genuinely occurred.

The key idea embedded in "pardon" is this: the wrong is acknowledged, not denied. Something did happen. But the person in a position to punish or resent chooses instead to let it go.

1. In Everyday Life — Forgiving a Fault

When you pardon someone in a personal, human sense, you forgive them for a mistake, a rudeness, or an offense. You decide not to stay angry or hold a grudge.

  • "She pardoned her friend for forgetting her birthday."
  • "He couldn't bring himself to pardon his brother for the betrayal."

Here, pardoning is an act of grace. You had every right to be upset, but you choose to let it go.

2. In Law and Government — An Official Release from Punishment

This is one of the most important uses of the word. When a head of state — a president, a king, a governor — pardons someone, they officially cancel that person's legal punishment. The person may have been convicted of a crime, but the authority steps in and says: "This person will not serve this sentence."

  • "The president pardoned the soldier before he could be executed."
  • "After new evidence came to light, the governor pardoned the wrongfully convicted man."

This is a powerful, formal act. A crucial point to understand here: a pardon does not mean the person is declared innocent. It does not erase guilt or overturn a conviction (unless the legal system specifically says so). It simply lifts the punishment. The record of the crime may still exist — but the consequence is removed.

Think of it this way: a judge says "you are guilty and must serve ten years." A pardon says "you will not serve those ten years" — but it doesn't say "you didn't do it."

3. Social Politeness — "Pardon Me"

You use "pardon me" to politely excuse a small, socially awkward action — interrupting someone, accidentally bumping into them, passing in front of them, sneezing, or saying something that might have been rude.

  • "Pardon me for interrupting, but the meeting starts in two minutes."
  • "Oh, pardon me!" (said after bumping into a stranger)
  • "Pardon me for saying this, but I think you have the wrong address."

In this use, you are essentially asking the other person to excuse a minor inconvenience or offense — a small request for grace. It signals politeness and awareness of social norms.

4. "Pardon?" — Asking Someone to Repeat Themselves

When used alone as a question, "Pardon?" is a polite way of asking someone to say something again because you didn't hear or understand them.

  • "Pardon? Could you speak a little louder?"
  • "Pardon? I'm afraid I didn't catch that."

This is softer and more polite than saying "What?" or "Huh?" It signals respect for the other person while acknowledging you missed what they said.
The Common Thread Across All Uses

Whether you're forgiving a friend, releasing a prisoner from a sentence, excusing yourself after interrupting, or asking someone to repeat themselves — every use of "pardon" shares one idea:

A small or large act of grace, in which someone is released from a consequence, a judgment, or an awkwardness.

The word always carries a sense of one person extending leniency or consideration to another.

Understanding what makes "pardon" different from close words will sharpen your understanding significantly.

Pardon vs. Forgive:
Both involve letting go of a wrong. But forgive is emotional and internal — it's about releasing resentment from your heart. Pardon is more formal and external — it's about releasing someone from consequences or blame. A judge can pardon a criminal (a formal, official act) without personally forgiving them in their heart. A mother can forgive her child emotionally without formally pardoning any consequence. In casual everyday speech, people use them almost interchangeably — but in formal or legal language, "pardon" is the correct word.

Pardon vs. Excuse:
These are very close in the social sense. "Excuse me" and "pardon me" are both used for minor inconveniences. But "pardon" tends to feel slightly more formal and deliberate. If you bump into someone on the street, both work. But if you want to interrupt a formal meeting or address someone of higher status, "pardon me" feels more appropriate. "Excuse" is also often used to justify behaviour ("She excused her lateness by blaming traffic"), while "pardon" is not normally used that way.

Pardon vs. Acquit:
This distinction is legally critical. To acquit someone means a court has determined they are not guilty — they didn't commit the crime. To pardon someone means they may well have committed it, but they are being released from punishment anyway. These are fundamentally different outcomes. An acquittal says "innocent." A pardon says "guilty, but freed."

"Pardon" is a word that naturally leans toward the formal side. In very casual speech, people more often say "forgive," "let it go," or just "no worries." But "pardon" becomes the right word in formal writing, legal contexts, official situations, and polite social interactions where you want to sound respectful and measured.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

To pardon someone is to extend a deliberate act of mercy or leniency — to decide that a wrong, an offense, or an inconvenience will not be punished, resented, or held against a person. It can happen on a grand, official scale (a head of state releasing a prisoner) or on a small, human scale (asking someone to forgive you for bumping their shoulder). The word always implies that something happened, that the person pardoning has the standing to respond to it, and that they choose grace over consequence.
11914:
To pare means to carefully cut away or remove the outer layer of something, usually with a blade or knife. Think of someone sitting at a kitchen table, slowly running a knife along the skin of an apple, removing just the thin outer layer — that is paring.

The key idea here is removing what is on the outside or on top — the excess, the covering, the unwanted layer — with precision and care, leaving behind the essential part underneath.

1. The Literal Use — With Food (or Similar Things)

In its most common, everyday sense, you pare a fruit or vegetable when you cut its skin off with a knife.

"She pared the potatoes before boiling them."
"He carefully pared the mango."
"The chef pared the apple in one long, continuous strip."

This is also where the term "paring knife" comes from — it's the small, short-bladed knife specifically designed for this task.

An important distinction from "peel":
"Peel" and "pare" are close, but not identical. You peel a banana with your fingers. You pare an apple with a knife. So "pare" specifically suggests a cutting or slicing action, usually with a tool. It also implies a degree of care and precision — you're not hacking at something, you're making deliberate, controlled cuts.

2. The Figurative Use — Cutting Things Down

This is where "pare" becomes truly powerful and widely used. In a non-food context, to pare means to reduce something gradually by cutting away what is unnecessary, excessive, or unwanted — to strip something down to what really matters.

Think of it this way: just as you pare an apple by removing everything that isn't the apple itself, you can "pare" a budget by removing everything that isn't essential spending.

"The company had to pare its costs after a difficult year."
"She pared her schedule down to just the most important meetings."
"The editor helped him pare the essay — it went from 10 pages to 4 sharp, focused ones."
"They pared the list of candidates from fifty to six."

The idea is always gradual, careful reduction — not a sudden, dramatic slash, but a thoughtful trimming, layer by layer, until you're left with the core.

These multi-word combinations with "pare" are very common, especially in writing and news:

Pare down — The most common combination. It means to reduce something, often repeatedly or gradually, until it reaches a smaller, cleaner, more essential form.

"We need to pare down our expenses."
"She pared down her wardrobe to only what she truly wore."

Pare back — Very similar to "pare down." Often used in business, politics, or planning to mean reducing the scale or ambition of something.

"The government pared back its spending plans."
"They pared back the original proposal significantly."

Pare away — Suggests removing layers, one by one, until something unnecessary is gone.

"Years of therapy helped him pare away the anxiety and find clarity."
"The sculptor pared away the excess stone to reveal the figure within."

In all of these, the common thread is: removing to improve, simplify, or reduce.

One thing that makes "pare" special compared to words like "cut" or "reduce" is its tone. It suggests:

  • Precision, not recklessness
  • Gradual removal, not a sudden chop
  • Intentionality — you know what you're keeping and what you're removing
  • A sense of refinement — you are making something leaner, cleaner, better

When someone says a writer "pared the novel down," it's almost a compliment — it means the writer carefully removed everything that didn't belong until only the good stuff remained.
Watch Out — Three Words That Sound Identical

This is crucial for a learner: "pare," "pear," and "pair" all sound exactly the same in English. They are homophones — same sound, completely different meanings.

  • Pare (verb) — to cut/trim/reduce
  • Pear (noun) — the fruit 🍐
  • Pair (noun/verb) — two matching things, or to put two things together

When you see them written, the spelling tells you which one is meant. In spoken English, context does that job.

SituationWhat "pare" means

In one sentence: "Pare" means to carefully cut away an outer layer or to gradually reduce something down to its most essential form. Whether you're peeling a vegetable or trimming a budget, the word always carries the idea of deliberate, careful removal — of stripping away the unnecessary to leave behind what truly matters.
11915: Paregoric is a specific type of liquid medicine that contains opium as its main active ingredient. More precisely, it is what pharmacists call a camphorated tincture of opium — meaning opium dissolved in alcohol and combined with a few other ingredients, notably camphor and anise oil.

A tincture is just a medicine made by dissolving a substance in alcohol. Think of it as a medicated liquid — not a pill, not a syrup, but a thin, alcohol-based solution you take in drops or small spoonfuls.

The opium in it comes from the same plant that gives us morphine and codeine. Opium is the dried sap of the poppy plant, and it has two powerful effects on the human body: it relieves pain, and it dramatically slows down the movement of the gut. That second effect is what made paregoric so useful historically.

Paregoric was used primarily as a treatment for diarrhea. Because opium slows intestinal movement, it stops the gut from pushing its contents through too fast — which is exactly what you want when someone has severe diarrhea.

Beyond diarrhea, it was also used for:

  • Stomach cramps and intestinal pain (the opium acts as a painkiller)
  • Coughs (opium suppresses the cough reflex)
  • Teething pain in infants and children (this use is now considered extremely dangerous and is no longer acceptable — more on that below)
The Historical Context: A Medicine Cabinet Staple

For roughly two centuries — from the 1700s through the early 1900s — paregoric was one of the most widely used medicines in homes across Europe and North America. It was available without a prescription, sold freely in pharmacies and general stores, and treated almost like a home remedy rather than a drug. Families kept a bottle in the house the way people today might keep ibuprofen.

It was given to babies to calm them when they were teething. It was given to adults and children at the first sign of stomach trouble. It was used in very young infants to ease withdrawal symptoms if their mothers were addicted to opioids. Its role in everyday medicine was enormous.

The reason for its popularity was simple: it worked. Diarrhea in the 18th and 19th centuries was genuinely life-threatening, especially for children, who could die quickly from dehydration. Paregoric stopped diarrhea effectively. At a time when safe, reliable medicines were scarce, that made it incredibly valuable.

As medical understanding grew through the 20th century, the serious dangers of paregoric became impossible to ignore.

First, opium is addictive — and because paregoric was given freely, including to children and infants, it created dependency in people who often didn't even understand what they were taking. Many people in the 1800s were unknowingly addicted to opium-containing products like paregoric.

Second, giving paregoric to infants and very young children is dangerous. Their nervous systems are extremely sensitive to opioids, and even small doses can suppress breathing and cause death. The historical practice of rubbing paregoric on a teething baby's gums is now recognized as something that killed children.

Third, opium (and its derivatives) can cause sedation, respiratory depression (dangerously slow breathing), and overdose — particularly in the elderly, in people with certain health conditions, and when combined with alcohol or other medications.

Paregoric still exists as a recognized pharmaceutical product, but its status has changed dramatically. In the United States and most other countries, it is now a controlled substance — meaning you cannot get it without a prescription, and its distribution is closely regulated by the government, in the same legal category as other opioid medications.

In modern clinical medicine, it is rarely prescribed. Better and safer treatments for diarrhea exist — medicines like loperamide (Imodium) achieve a similar gut-slowing effect without the full risks of opium. Paregoric is occasionally still used in hospital settings to treat neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (when newborns are born dependent on opioids because their mothers used opioids during pregnancy), but even this use is being replaced by safer alternatives.

So paregoric went from being a ubiquitous household staple to a tightly controlled, rarely used relic of pharmaceutical history — a journey that mirrors society's growing understanding of opioid addiction and danger.
The Broader Significance of Knowing This Word

Paregoric appears frequently in historical literature, medical texts from the 18th and 19th centuries, and discussions of the history of drug policy and opioid epidemics. When you encounter the word in those contexts, it signals a world where opium-based medicines were casually handed out like aspirin — a reminder that the opioid crisis is not entirely a modern invention, but has roots in centuries of widespread, under-regulated opium use.

It also appears in legal and pharmacological texts when discussing the history of drug scheduling and regulation, since products like paregoric were among the first medicines to be brought under legal control as governments began recognizing the public health dangers of freely available opioids.

Paregoric (noun) = a liquid opium-based medicine, historically used to treat diarrhea, stomach pain, and coughs. It was a common household medicine for centuries, given even to infants, before its dangers as an addictive opioid substance were fully understood. Today it is a controlled substance, rarely used, and largely replaced by safer modern alternatives.
11916:
Something parenthetical is extra. It is information added into a sentence or a piece of writing as a side note, an aside, or a small detour — information that is useful or interesting, but not essential. The main sentence can stand perfectly well without it.

Think of it like a whisper inside a conversation. While telling a story, if you pause to add "by the way" or "just so you know" and then return to your story — that interjection is parenthetical. It enriches what you're saying, but your story survives without it.

The word "parenthetical" is inseparable from the punctuation marks called parentheses — the curved brackets: ( ). Whatever sits inside those brackets is, by definition, parenthetical. The brackets are a signal to the reader: this is extra — not the main point.

My sister (who studied in Paris) just got a promotion.

The main sentence is: "My sister just got a promotion." The bracketed part — who studied in Paris — only adds extra context. It is parenthetical.

The most reliable way to decide whether something is parenthetical is to ask yourself: "If I remove this, does the sentence still make complete sense?"

If yes → it is parenthetical. It's extra.
If no → it is essential. Not parenthetical.

Take these two sentences:

"The storm, which lasted three days, destroyed the harbor."

Remove which lasted three days → "The storm destroyed the harbor." Still complete and sensible. That clause is parenthetical — it gives bonus detail about the storm.

"The storm that destroyed the harbor began in the south."

Remove that destroyed the harbor → "The storm began in the south." Grammatically okay, but now you've lost the specific storm being referred to. That clause identifies which storm is meant — it is essential, and therefore not parenthetical.

This is important: parenthetical does not only mean "inside brackets." A piece of information can be parenthetical in spirit — even if no brackets are used. Writers signal parenthetical elements in three common ways, and all three are equally valid:

Using parentheses: She passed her exam (after three attempts) and celebrated all night.
Using dashes: She passed her exam — after three attempts — and celebrated all night.
Using commas: She passed her exam, after three attempts, and celebrated all night.

In all three versions, after three attempts is parenthetical. The choice of punctuation only changes the tone — parentheses feel like a quiet aside, dashes feel more emphatic and dramatic, and commas blend the aside most smoothly into the sentence.

"Parenthetical" also describes a quality of speech or thought — a tendency to insert side comments, qualifications, or digressions while making a point.

"He was — and I say this with great affection — the most chaotic person I've ever met."

The phrase and I say this with great affection is a parenthetical remark. It's a conversational detour slipped into the middle of a sentence. It softens or qualifies what's being said, and then the speaker returns to their main thought.

People and writers who tend to add lots of asides, footnotes, qualifications, or extra details could be described as having a parenthetical style. Their thinking meanders productively — they always have something extra to add.

Writers use parenthetical remarks to: clarify something mid-sentence, add a humorous aside, soften a strong statement, or give the reader background they might need.

In a more critical or rhetorical context, calling something "parenthetical" can gently imply it is minor or even beside the point.

"That concern is parenthetical to the real argument."

This means: that concern is a sideshow — it doesn't belong at the center of the discussion. It's like saying it should be in the footnotes, not the main text. The word isn't cruel here, but it does push something to the edges.

In everyday use, "parenthetical" most commonly modifies words like these:

A parenthetical remark is a comment made in passing, not the central point being made.
A parenthetical comment is much the same — a side observation dropped into conversation or writing.
A parenthetical aside is a brief digression from the main thought.
A parenthetical phrase or parenthetical clause refers, in grammar, to a group of words inserted into a sentence as extra — non-essential — information.
A parenthetical note is a supplementary detail added in writing.

You will also encounter the adverb parenthetically, which means "by way of a side remark" or "as an aside." It's used when a speaker or writer wants to signal that what follows is not the main point:

"Parenthetically, I should mention that we ran out of funding halfway through."

It's the verbal equivalent of leaning in and whispering something before returning to the main conversation.

Parenthetical means: secondary, extra, inserted as an aside, and removable without breaking the main meaning. Whether it describes a phrase inside brackets, a remark dropped into a sentence mid-thought, or a quality of someone's speech, the idea is the same — it is information that lives beside the main point, not at the heart of it. It supplements, qualifies, clarifies, or digresses — and the world (or at least the sentence) keeps going fine without it.
11917: A parfait is a dessert. But here's the interesting thing — the word actually refers to two quite different desserts, depending on whether you're talking about French cuisine or American cuisine. Both share the name, but they look and taste quite different from each other. To truly understand the word, you need to know both.

In its original, classical sense, a parfait is a frozen dessert made from three main ingredients: egg yolks, sugar, and heavy cream.

Here's the basic idea of how it comes together: the egg yolks and sugar are cooked together into a thick, rich, custard-like mixture. Then, whipped cream is folded into this mixture. The whole thing is then poured into a mold — often a loaf-shaped mold — and left to freeze solid, without being stirred or churned at any point.

That last detail is important. Unlike ice cream, which has to be churned constantly while freezing (to keep it smooth and creamy), a parfait is simply left to freeze on its own, untouched. This works because the fat from the whipped cream and the air whipped into it are enough to give it a naturally smooth, silky texture without any churning. The result is a dense, rich, intensely creamy frozen dessert.

When it's ready, the frozen parfait is sliced into individual portions and served on a plate, much like you'd slice a cake or a loaf of bread. It holds its shape firmly.

The flavor of a French parfait depends on what's added to it. Common flavors include coffee, chocolate, praline (caramelized nuts), vanilla, and various fruit purées. These are added to the base mixture before freezing, and they define the character of the dessert. A coffee parfait, for example, will taste deeply, richly of coffee — more intensely than most frozen desserts, because the dense, creamy base carries flavor beautifully.

The texture of a French parfait is something between very rich ice cream and a frozen mousse. It's smooth, not icy, and it melts luxuriously on your tongue. Because of the high cream and egg content, it has a heavier, more indulgent feel than regular ice cream.

In the United States, the word "parfait" took on a completely different meaning over time. An American parfait is not frozen solid. It's a layered dessert, assembled in a tall, clear glass so that the layers are visible from the outside.

The layers typically alternate between something creamy (like ice cream, whipped cream, or yogurt), something fruity (like fresh berries, sliced peaches, or fruit compote), and something crunchy (like granola, crushed cookies, or nuts). These layers are stacked on top of each other inside the glass, creating a striped, colorful appearance that makes the dessert visually appealing before you even take a bite.

There are two common types of American parfaits:

Dessert parfaits use ice cream as the creamy base, often paired with chocolate or caramel sauce, whipped cream, and a cherry on top. Think of it as a more elaborate, layered version of an ice cream sundae.

Yogurt parfaits use yogurt — often Greek yogurt — as the creamy layer, paired with fresh fruit and granola. This version is lighter and less sweet, and it's commonly eaten as a breakfast or a healthy snack, not just as a dessert.

The experience of eating an American parfait is different from eating a French one. Since it's not frozen solid, the textures are varied and contrasting within each bite — creamy, crunchy, and fruity all at once. The tall glass it's served in is also part of the identity of this dessert; you can see every layer through the glass, which makes it look elegant and carefully assembled.

Both types of parfait share a sense of richness and care in how they're made. The French parfait represents classical technique — a controlled, labor-intensive process producing something dense and refined. The American parfait represents abundance and visual appeal — something layered, generous, and immediately impressive to look at.

If you encounter the word "parfait" in a French restaurant or in the context of classical cooking, it almost certainly refers to the frozen, molded version. If you see it on a diner menu, a breakfast menu, or at a café in the United States, it almost certainly refers to the layered dessert in a glass.
A Few Extra Details Worth Knowing

• A parfait is always served cold. The French version comes out of the freezer; the American version is typically chilled and often contains something frozen (like ice cream) within its layers.
  • The word "parfait" is used in English exactly as it is — it's borrowed directly from French and has not been anglicized. You'll see it written as "parfait" in English menus and cookbooks, not translated into anything else.
  • In everyday American English, when someone says "I had a parfait," they almost always mean the layered yogurt or ice cream version. The French frozen parfait is rarely encountered outside of fine dining or formal cooking contexts.
  • Yogurt parfaits are extremely common in the United States and are considered an everyday food, not a special-occasion dessert. You'll find them pre-packaged in grocery stores, served at hotel breakfasts, and made fresh at cafés.

In short: a parfait is a dessert — either a rich, frozen, molded cream dessert from French cuisine, or a layered, visually striking dessert served in a tall glass in American cuisine. Both are cold, both are indulgent in their own way, and both are considered elegant or appealing presentations of their ingredients.
11918:
A pariah is a person — or sometimes a group, organization, or country — that is completely rejected, shunned, and avoided by the people or society around them. They are treated as an outcast: someone who is cut off from the group, unwelcome, and deliberately kept at a distance.

Think of it this way: imagine a community where everyone collectively turns their back on one person. Nobody wants to be seen with them. Nobody includes them. Nobody defends them. That person is a pariah.

A pariah isn't simply someone who is shy, lonely, or unpopular. The key difference is that a pariah's isolation comes from the outside — from other people actively choosing to exclude them.

This rejection usually happens for one of two reasons:

1. Something the person actually did. A politician caught in a massive corruption scandal might become a pariah in political circles. Someone who betrayed a close community might be shunned by everyone in it. A public figure who said something deeply offensive might find that nobody wants to associate with them anymore. The action caused real damage — to trust, to morals, to relationships — and the community responds by casting the person out.

2. Something others believe about the person — fairly or unfairly. This is where the word gets more powerful and tragic. Throughout history, people have been made pariahs not because of anything they truly did wrong, but because of prejudice, fear, or misunderstanding. They were labeled as "different," "dangerous," or "lesser," and society treated them accordingly — excluding them, refusing to interact with them, treating them as if their very presence were a problem.

Both cases share the same result: the person is pushed to the edges of social life and left there.

This is important: being a pariah is not a mild or casual form of dislike. It is total social exclusion. The word carries a sense of someone being treated as though they are untouchable — as if simply associating with them would taint or harm you.

Compare these three situations:

  • Unpopular person → People don't seek them out, but they're still included in everyday life.
  • Outcast → People avoid them; they are on the fringe of the group.
  • Pariah → People go out of their way to exclude and shun them; their presence itself is unwanted. This is the strongest level.

A pariah is at the far end of this scale. The rejection is total, deliberate, and often public.
It Doesn't Only Apply to People

While "pariah" most commonly describes an individual, it can also be applied to:

  • Groups or organizations — A company found guilty of massive fraud might become a pariah in its industry. No one wants to do business with it.
  • Countries — A nation that violates international law, wages illegal wars, or commits mass atrocities can become a pariah state — a country that is isolated, condemned, and shut out by the international community. Other nations refuse to trade with it, recognize it diplomatically, or cooperate with it.

The word scales up naturally, because the core idea — being rejected and excluded by a wider community — applies whether that community is a neighborhood or the entire world.
The Emotional and Moral Weight of the Word

"Pariah" is not a neutral word. It is heavy with judgment. When you call someone a pariah, you are communicating that:

  • Their exclusion is complete, not partial.
  • Their exclusion is recognized — it's not a private opinion; it's a shared social reality.
  • There is often a sense of disgrace attached to them — something about them is considered unacceptable, shameful, or contaminating to those around them.

Because of this weight, the word is often used deliberately for emphasis, to convey just how severe someone's social or moral fall has been.
Common Ways the Word Is Used

• "After the scandal broke, he became a pariah in the industry — no one would return his calls."
  • "She had spoken an uncomfortable truth, and for it, she was treated like a pariah by her own colleagues."
  • "The regime's actions turned it into an international pariah, cut off from trade and diplomacy."
  • "He was once celebrated; now he was a social pariah."

Notice how the word always signals a dramatic fall — from belonging to complete exclusion.
How It Differs from Similar Words

WordHow it differs from "pariah"
OutcastBroader and more neutral; a pariah carries a stronger sense of active shunning and disgrace
ExileImplies physical removal from a place; a pariah suffers social rejection, not necessarily physical removal
LonerA loner often chooses isolation; a pariah has isolation forced upon them by others
Persona non grataA formal term for someone unwelcome in a specific context; "pariah" is broader and more emotionally charged
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you walk away with one clear idea, let it be this:

A pariah is someone that a community — big or small — has collectively decided to reject, avoid, and treat as unwanted. The rejection isn't quiet or accidental. It is deliberate, widespread, and total. The pariah is cast out, treated as untouchable, and left on the outside of social life.

That sense of total, active, collective exclusion — with all its shame and isolation — is the beating heart of this word.
11919: A parish is a small, defined local community and the geographic area it occupies, managed or cared for by a specific authority. That authority is either a church (in the religious sense) or a local government (in the civil sense). Both meanings share the same fundamental idea: a clearly bounded local area and the people living within it.

In Christianity, a parish is a specific geographic district assigned to a single local church and its priest or minister. The church is responsible for the spiritual care of everyone living within that district.

Think of it this way: imagine a city divided into invisible zones drawn on a map. Each zone has one church assigned to it. That church looks after all the people in its zone — conducting services, performing baptisms, officiating weddings and funerals, and so on. Each of those zones is a parish.

Now here is something important: the word "parish" carries a double meaning even within religion. It refers to:

  • The area itself — the defined territory or district. ("There are five schools in the parish.")
  • The people living in that area — the local community or congregation. ("The whole parish turned out for the festival.")

You will regularly see it used both ways, and context will always make it clear which meaning is intended.

Parishes are found across many Christian denominations — Roman Catholic, Anglican (Church of England), Episcopal, Lutheran, and others — but the term is most strongly associated with the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of England. In these traditions, a group of several parishes together forms a larger unit called a diocese, which is overseen by a bishop. So the hierarchy goes: parish → diocese → and beyond.

The person in charge of a parish is typically called a parish priest (in Catholicism), a vicar or rector (in the Church of England), or simply a pastor (in many Protestant churches). They live and work within the parish they serve.

Separately from religion, parish is also used as an official unit of local government in certain places. This happened historically because early governments in many countries modeled their local administrative divisions on existing church parishes. Over time, the civil and religious uses separated, but the name stuck.

Here is where this civil meaning applies today:

England and Wales: A civil parish is the smallest official unit of local government — smaller than a district, which is smaller than a county. A civil parish might be a village, a small town, or a defined neighborhood. It has its own elected parish council that handles very local matters like maintaining village greens, local footpaths, street lighting, and community halls. These are entirely separate from religion now — they just kept the name.

Louisiana, USA: This is the most famous example outside England. Louisiana is the only US state that uses the word parish instead of "county" to divide itself. So while Texas has counties (like Harris County), Louisiana has parishes (like Orleans Parish or Jefferson Parish). There are 64 parishes in Louisiana. This comes from the state's deep Catholic French and Spanish colonial history, where the church parish and the local administrative unit were originally the same thing.

Jamaica: The island nation of Jamaica is divided into 14 parishes, such as Kingston, St. Andrew, and St. James. These are the main administrative divisions of the country, roughly equivalent to counties or provinces elsewhere.

This is worth knowing because you will encounter it in history and genealogy. Before governments kept official records of births, deaths, and marriages, churches did. These records — called parish records or parish registers — were kept by the local parish priest and are among the most important historical documents that exist for tracing family histories, especially in Europe. When historians or genealogists say they "searched the parish records," they mean these old church registers.

One of the most natural and common uses of "parish" is to refer to the people of a community, not just the place. This is important to internalize because it can catch learners off guard.

  • "The priest gave a sermon to his parish." → He spoke to the people of his congregation/community.
  • "The parish raised funds for the new roof." → The community of people raised funds.
  • "She is well-known throughout the parish." → Everyone in that local community knows her.

In this way, "parish" functions much like the word "community" — it is both a place and the people in it at the same time.

Parish always means the same thing: a small, defined local unit — both the area and the people in it — under the care of a specific authority.

  • Religiously: it is the local church district, served by one priest or minister, belonging to a larger diocese.
  • Civilly: it is the smallest unit of local government (England/Wales), or the equivalent of a county (Louisiana), or a main regional division (Jamaica).
  • In everyday use: it refers naturally to the community of people in that area, not just the land itself.

The word is rooted in the idea of something local, intimate, and community-based — a small world with its own identity, its own people, and its own caretaker.
